title: With Due Respect (Vol. 7) -- Ch. 12: Japan, the New and the Old
keywords: Japan, the New and the Old
a country of contrasts and contradictions
primary_topics: Chapter 12 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7) -- CJP's June 24, 2007 Inquirer column, a travelogue of a Globus grand tour of Japan that followed his Tokyo trip to thank the Japanese government for a P300-million grant for the Philja Development Center

His impressions of 'high-tech Japan' -- the Shinkansen, the high-tech toilets and 'Pillow Menu,' the GPS-guided cars and the indecipherable 'chome' address system -- alongside fine wagyu and Hiroshima okonomiyaki

His reading of 'traditional Japan' -- the prizing of 'wa' (harmony), the absence of an exact 'no,' the 'gap between what is said and what is the truth,' and the rituals of calling cards, bowing and non-tipping

His portrait of 'democratic Japan' -- parliamentary, free-trading, with an independent Supreme Court and a Shinto-Buddhist-Christian blend -- a country of 'contrasts and contradictions' marrying 'oriental charm and Western innovations'
sub_topics: The occasion: after a Tokyo visit 'to thank the Japanese government for the P300-million unconditional grant' for the 'Philja Development Center in Tagaytay,' CJP and his wife Leni 'joined a grand tour of Japan arranged by Globus'

High-tech wonders: staying in 'Tokyo, Osaka, and Kyoto' and smaller cities, they rode the Shinkansen ('at 280 kilometers per hour... amazingly quiet and smooth,' fast enough to reach 'Baguio... from Manila in an hour'), used hotels with 'high-tech toilets' (heated seats, electronic bidets, air blowers), and chose from the Osaka Hilton's 'Pillow Menu' of six pillows (buckwheat 'sobagara,' cypress 'hinoko,' duck feather, 'tempur,' etc.)

Navigation and cuisine: cars carried 'global positioning systems' with voice guides 'so no driver would ever get lost' in a country that 'do[es] not give names to their streets' but uses a 'chome system... too complicated' for CJP -- and he savored wagyu at the Okura (hosted by Lehman Brothers' Carlos 'Pop' Mañalac) and 'reasonably priced' Hiroshima okonomiyaki he hoped 'an entrepreneur would introduce... in Makati'

Wa and harmony: 'despite being the second largest economy in the world, Japan still retains many vestiges of its past,' chief of which is 'wa,' or 'harmony' -- a society prizing 'group cohesion, teamwork, and consensus,' with 'no exact equivalent of the English word no' and where 'hai does not necessarily mean I agree' but often merely 'I understand'

Indirectness: because the Japanese 'hate to displease, there is almost always a gap between what is said and what is the truth' -- as when, coming late for a show, CJP was told not 'no' but that 'the weather was unpredictable' and 'the next day would probably bring in the sunshine,' an indirect 'come back the following day'

Courtesies: 'calling cards are extremely important... to show the rank and career status of the giver' (there being 'a distinct way of speaking with an inferior... a superior and... an equal'); 'tipping is not common' (waiters 'sometimes offended when tipped'); and bowing, 'customary,' can mean 'anything from hello to goodbye to thank you'

Democratic Japan: 'steadfastly parliamentary,' Japan is 'headed by a prime minister,' with lawmaking in 'a two-house Diet' and 'judicial power... exercised by an independent Supreme Court,' its people 'nonetheless entrepreneurial and committed to free trade'; its faiths are Shinto and Buddhism (about 2 percent Christian), so many Japanese 'are said to be born Shinto, marry Christian, and die Buddhist'

A country of contrasts: returning after a 25-year absence, CJP finds Japan 'still a country of contrasts and contradictions; an oasis of oriental charm and Western innovations; a cradle of Eastern religions and an exemplar of liberal democracy; a promoter of human rights and an adherent of free trade' that 'pioneers e-age technologies but retains its traditional values'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 12 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7), CJP's June 24, 2007 Inquirer column, is a travelogue of a Globus grand tour of Japan that followed his Tokyo trip 'to thank the Japanese government for the P300-million unconditional grant' for the 'Philja Development Center in Tagaytay.' In 'high-tech Japan,' he and his wife Leni rode the Shinkansen ('at 280 kilometers per hour... amazingly quiet and smooth,' fast enough to reach 'Baguio... from Manila in an hour'), used hotels with 'high-tech toilets' and an Osaka 'Pillow Menu' of six pillows, and rode GPS-guided cars through a land that uses an indecipherable 'chome' address system, savoring wagyu at the Okura and Hiroshima okonomiyaki. In 'traditional Japan,' 'despite being the second largest economy in the world,' the country keeps its past -- above all 'wa,' or 'harmony,' a value prizing 'group cohesion, teamwork, and consensus,' so there is 'no exact equivalent of the English word no,' 'hai' often means only 'I understand,' and 'there is almost always a gap between what is said and what is the truth' (coming late for a show, CJP was told the 'weather was unpredictable' -- an indirect 'come back tomorrow'). Calling cards signal 'rank and career status,' tipping 'is not common,' and bowing can mean 'anything from hello to goodbye.' In 'democratic Japan,' the country is 'steadfastly parliamentary,' with 'a two-house Diet,' 'an independent Supreme Court,' and a people 'entrepreneurial and committed to free trade,' their faiths Shinto and Buddhism (about 2 percent Christian), so many 'are said to be born Shinto, marry Christian, and die Buddhist.' Returning after 25 years, CJP finds Japan still 'a country of contrasts and contradictions; an oasis of oriental charm and Western innovations... a promoter of human rights and an adherent of free trade' that 'pioneers e-age technologies but retains its traditional values.'
